name: Memoization
overview: Memoization is a top-down dynamic programming technique that caches the results of expensive function calls and reuses them when the same inputs recur. It converts an exponential brute-force recursion into an efficient solution by storing computed subproblem answers.
why: Memoization is the most direct way to turn a naive recursive solution into a polynomial one, making it a favorite first step in interviews. Recognizing overlapping subproblems and caching them shows strong DP fundamentals.
when: Reach for memoization whenever you have a recursive solution that repeats work, especially one whose state can be described by a small tuple of integers. It is simplest when the state space is manageable and recursion depth is not a concern.

complexity.space: O(states) for the cache plus recursion stack

concepts.name: Overlapping Subproblems
concepts.description: Subproblems that are solved multiple times during recursion; caching their answers avoids redundant work.

concepts.name: Top-Down
concepts.description: Starting from the full problem and recursively breaking it down to base cases.

concepts.name: State Key
concepts.description: The tuple of function parameters that uniquely identifies a subproblem and acts as the cache key.

concepts.name: Base Case
concepts.description: The smallest input for which the answer is known directly, terminating the recursion.

concepts.name: Recursion Stack
concepts.description: The call stack overhead; deep recursion can cause stack overflow in iterative languages.

patterns.name: Standard Memoized Recursion
patterns.description: Check the cache, compute recursively if missing, store and return.

patterns.name: Manual Dictionary Cache
patterns.description: Use a dict or array as a cache when lru_cache is unavailable or state is multi-dimensional.

examples.title: Fibonacci with Memoization
examples.problem: Compute the nth Fibonacci number where fib(0)=0, fib(1)=1, and fib(n)=fib(n-1)+fib(n-2).
examples.explanation: Naive recursion recomputes fib for the same n many times. Memoization stores each result once, reducing the work to O(n).
steps: Define the recursive function with a base case for n <= 1.
Before recursing, check if f(n) is already in the cache.
If not, compute f(n-1) + f(n-2) recursively and store it.
Return the cached value.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the base case, causing infinite recursion.
mistakes.fix: Always define and return the base case before anything else.

mistakes.mistake: Caching on only part of the state, producing wrong answers for multi-parameter problems.
mistakes.fix: Use every parameter that affects the result in the cache key.

mistakes.mistake: Using recursion on very deep state spaces and hitting stack overflow.
mistakes.fix: Either increase recursion limits or switch to an iterative bottom-up approach.

problems.name: Fibonacci Number
problems.description: Return the nth Fibonacci number where F(0)=0, F(1)=1.
problems.approach: Memoize the recursive definition so each F(i) is computed once.
problems.solution: Recurse with memoization: return i for i<=1, otherwise return cached sum of the two previous values.

problems.name: Climbing Stairs
problems.description: You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count the distinct ways to reach the top of n stairs.
hints: The ways to reach step i equals ways to i-1 plus ways to i-2.
problems.approach: The recurrence is Fibonacci-like; memoize dp(i) = dp(i-1) + dp(i-2).
problems.solution: dp(i) counts ways to climb i stairs with base cases dp(0)=1 and dp(1)=1, caching each state.

problems.name: House Robber
problems.description: Rob houses along a street without robbing two adjacent ones; return the maximum amount you can rob.
hints: At each house, decide to rob it or skip it.
State is just the current index.
problems.approach: Memoize dp(i) = max(dp(i+1), nums[i] + dp(i+2)).
problems.solution: At each house choose between skipping it or taking it plus the result two houses later; cache the answer per index.

name: Tabulation
overview: Tabulation is the bottom-up form of dynamic programming that fills a table iteratively from base cases to the final answer. It avoids recursion overhead and often allows space optimization to a few rolling variables.
why: Interviewers expect you to translate a memoized recursion into an iterative table to show you understand the recurrence fully. Tabulation is also the safer choice when the state space is large and recursion depth is a limit.
when: Use tabulation when you can order subproblems so each depends only on already-computed smaller ones. It is ideal when the state space is dense (most states are used) rather than sparse.

complexity.space: O(states), often reducible to O(1) or O(n)

concepts.name: Bottom-Up
concepts.description: Starting from the smallest subproblems and building up to the full problem.

concepts.name: DP Table
concepts.description: An array or matrix where each cell stores the answer for a subproblem.

concepts.name: Base Case Initialization
concepts.description: Filling in the starting values of the table before iterating.

concepts.name: Transition Order
concepts.description: The loop order that guarantees dependencies are computed before use.

concepts.name: Space Optimization
concepts.description: Keeping only the last few rows instead of the whole table when only recent values matter.

patterns.name: Iterative 1D Fill
patterns.description: Fill a one-dimensional table in order, each cell depending on earlier cells.

patterns.name: Rolling Array
patterns.description: Replace the table with two or three variables to cut space to O(1).

examples.title: Climbing Stairs via Tabulation
examples.problem: Count the number of distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps at a time.
examples.explanation: The recurrence dp(i)=dp(i-1)+dp(i-2) is filled left to right starting from dp(0)=dp(1)=1.
steps: Initialize dp[0] = 1 and dp[1] = 1.
Loop i from 2 to n.
Set dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].
Return dp[n].

mistakes.mistake: Filling the table in the wrong order so dependencies are not computed yet.
mistakes.fix: Analyze which states each cell depends on and iterate in dependency order.

mistakes.mistake: Wrong or missing base cases, corrupting every later cell.
mistakes.fix: Write down the base case for the smallest valid inputs and verify a couple of early cells by hand.

mistakes.mistake: Keeping a full table when only the last two rows are needed.
mistakes.fix: Use rolling variables to reduce memory to O(1).

problems.name: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
problems.description: Each step i has a cost; you can start at step 0 or 1 and pay cost[i] to leave. Return the minimum cost to reach the top.
hints: dp[i] is the minimum cost to reach step i.
You come from i-1 or i-2.
problems.approach: Tabulate dp[i] = cost[i] + min(dp[i-1], dp[i-2]).
problems.solution: Keep only the previous two minimum costs as rolling variables and return the min of the last two.

problems.name: Unique Paths
problems.description: Count paths from the top-left to bottom-right of an m x n grid moving only down or right.
hints: Each cell is reachable from above or the left.
problems.approach: Tabulate a grid where dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j] + dp[i][j-1].
problems.solution: Fill row by row, each cell summing the cell above and the cell to the left; the answer is the bottom-right cell.

problems.name: Coin Change
problems.description: Return the fewest number of coins from denominations that sum to a given amount, or -1 if impossible.
hints: dp[a] is the minimum coins for amount a.
Try every coin as the last one.
problems.approach: Tabulate dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - coin] for amounts 0..amount.
problems.solution: Initialize dp[0]=0 and the rest to infinity; for each amount try every coin and keep the minimum.

name: 1D DP
overview: 1D DP uses a one-dimensional array where each position represents the optimal value for a subproblem defined by a single index. The state is usually a position in an array or the length of a prefix.
why: 1D DP is the most frequently tested DP category and appears in easy and medium questions in nearly every interview. Mastering it builds the intuition for recurrence design used across all DP.
when: Reach for 1D DP when the only thing that changes between subproblems is a single integer such as an index, a length, or a target value. If the recurrence only needs the previous one or two cells, use rolling variables.

concepts.name: State
concepts.description: A single index i that defines the subproblem, such as the first i elements.

concepts.name: Recurrence
concepts.description: A formula expressing dp[i] in terms of earlier dp values.

concepts.name: Local vs Global Optimum
concepts.description: Tracking both the best value ending at i and the best seen so far.

concepts.name: Rolling Variables
concepts.description: Reusing a few variables to replace the full array.

concepts.name: Two-Pointer Style Transitions
concepts.description: Choosing between taking the current element or skipping it.

patterns.name: Max Subarray (Kadane)
patterns.description: Best sum ending at i is max of starting fresh or extending the previous segment.

patterns.name: Take or Skip
patterns.description: At each element decide to include it (with the constraint) or skip it.

examples.title: Maximum Subarray Sum
examples.problem: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum.
examples.explanation: Kadane's algorithm keeps the best sum ending at each position and the best overall, using a rolling variable.
steps: Initialize best and current with the first element.
For each next element, current = max(x, current + x).
Update best = max(best, current).
Return best.

mistakes.mistake: Initializing best to 0, which fails when all numbers are negative.
mistakes.fix: Initialize best and current to the first element, not 0.

mistakes.mistake: Mixing up take-or-skip base cases and allowing adjacent picks.
mistakes.fix: Rewrite the recurrence so each choice respects the constraint, then verify on a small example.

mistakes.mistake: Using a full array when only the last one or two values are needed.
mistakes.fix: Convert to rolling variables after deriving the recurrence.

problems.name: Maximum Subarray
problems.description: Find the contiguous subarray with the largest sum and return that sum.
hints: Track the best sum ending at each position.
A running sum reset when it goes negative works.
problems.approach: Use Kadane's algorithm with rolling variables.
problems.solution: Keep current best ending at i and global best; extend or restart the subarray at each step.

problems.name: Decode Ways
problems.description: Count the number of ways to decode a digit string where A=1..Z=26.
hints: dp[i] depends on decoding one or two digits at the end.
problems.approach: dp[i] = dp[i-1] (if one digit valid) + dp[i-2] (if two digits valid).
problems.solution: Slide two rolling values; add dp[i-1] when the last digit is non-zero and dp[i-2] when the last two form a valid 10..26.

problems.name: Word Break
problems.description: Return true if the string can be segmented into words from the dictionary.
hints: Check each dictionary word ending at i.
problems.approach: dp[i] is true if some valid word ends at i and dp[i-len(word)] is true.
problems.solution: Mark dp[0]=true; for each end position check every dictionary word that matches and is preceded by a true prefix.

name: 2D DP
overview: 2D DP keeps answers in a matrix where two dimensions describe the subproblem state, such as positions in two arrays or a position and a remaining capacity. It is the workhorse for string and grid problems.
why: 2D DP appears constantly in interviews covering grid paths, edit distance, and matching problems. Knowing how to set up the table and its boundaries separates strong candidates from average ones.
when: Use 2D DP when two independent quantities change together, like the lengths of two prefixes, an index and a budget, or a start and end in an interval. Watch for space optimization down to a single row when transitions only look left/up.

complexity.space: O(m * n), often optimizable to O(min(m, n))

concepts.name: Two State Dimensions
concepts.description: Each cell (i, j) represents a subproblem parameterized by two values.

concepts.name: Boundary Handling
concepts.description: Filling row 0 and column 0 correctly since they have no earlier neighbors.

concepts.name: Direction of Filling
concepts.description: Ordering loops so dependencies (up, left, diagonal) are ready.

concepts.name: Row Optimization
concepts.description: Reusing one array because a cell only needs the current and previous rows.

concepts.name: Path Reconstruction
concepts.description: Walking back through the table from the answer to recover the actual solution.

patterns.name: Grid Accumulation
patterns.description: Each cell's value comes from above, left, or diagonal neighbors.

patterns.name: Edit-Style Alignment
patterns.description: Compare two sequences and pay costs for matching, inserting, or deleting.

examples.title: Minimum Path Sum
examples.problem: Find a path from top-left to bottom-right moving only down or right that minimizes the sum of cell values.
examples.explanation: Each cell's minimum is its own value plus the smaller of the cell above and the cell to the left.
steps: Create a dp table the size of the grid.
Fill the first row and first column with prefix sums.
For interior cells take the min of top and left plus the cell value.
Return the bottom-right cell.

mistakes.mistake: Indexing out of bounds when checking the top or left neighbor in row 0 or column 0.
mistakes.fix: Handle the first row and column as a special prefix-sum case before the main loop.

mistakes.mistake: Using O(m*n) space when only the previous row is needed.
mistakes.fix: Keep a single row array and update it in place, tracking the diagonal value separately.

mistakes.mistake: Wrong loop order causing use of stale cells.
mistakes.fix: Fill in dependency order: top-to-bottom and left-to-right.

problems.name: Minimum Path Sum
problems.description: Return the minimum sum along a path from the top-left to bottom-right moving only down or right.
hints: dp[i][j] comes from above or left.
problems.approach: Accumulate each cell as its value plus the min of the two predecessors.
problems.solution: Fill the grid with prefix sums for the edges and the min recurrence for interiors.

problems.name: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.description: Return the length of the longest subsequence common to two strings.
hints: Match characters at i and j or skip one side.
problems.approach: LCS recurrence: if characters match take diagonal plus one, else take the max of skipping either.
problems.solution: Build a prefix table where matching chars extend the diagonal and mismatches carry the larger of the two neighbors.

problems.name: Edit Distance
problems.description: Return the minimum number of insert, delete, and replace operations to convert word1 into word2.
hints: Replace, insert, and delete are three costs.
problems.approach: dp[i][j] = min of diagonal (replace/match), up (delete), left (insert) plus one where needed.
problems.solution: Initialize the first row and column as costs of insertion/deletion, then apply the min-cost recurrence for each cell.

name: Knapsack
overview: Knapsack DP selects a subset of items, each with weight and value, to maximize value without exceeding a capacity. Its 0/1 and unbounded variants model a huge family of resource-allocation problems.
why: Knapsack is one of the most commonly asked DP families and its template generalizes to partition, subset-sum, and many optimization problems. Interviewers use it to test whether you can map a word problem onto a known state definition.
when: Reach for knapsack DP when you must choose items to fill a budget, capacity, or target, and each item is either taken (0/1) or can be repeated (unbounded). The state is (index or items processed, remaining capacity).

concepts.name: Capacity State
concepts.description: The second DP dimension tracks the remaining weight or budget.

concepts.name: 0/1 vs Unbounded
concepts.description: 0/1 allows at most one copy per item; unbounded allows unlimited copies, changing the loop direction.

concepts.name: Item Processing
concepts.description: Processing items one by one to avoid reusing an item in the 0/1 case.

concepts.name: Value vs Count Objective
concepts.description: Maximizing total value or counting the number of ways to reach a target.

concepts.name: 1D Space Reduction
concepts.description: Collapsing the 2D table into one array keyed by capacity.

patterns.name: 0/1 Knapsack
patterns.description: Decide include or exclude each item; iterate capacity backwards to avoid reuse.

patterns.name: Unbounded Knapsack
patterns.description: Iterate capacity forwards so each item can be reused.

examples.title: 0/1 Knapsack
examples.problem: Given weights [1,3,4,5] and values [1,4,5,7] with capacity 7, maximize total value.
examples.explanation: Choosing weights 3 and 4 gives value 4+5=9, the best combination under capacity 7.
steps: Initialize dp[0..7] to 0.
Process each item and update capacities from 7 down to its weight.
For each capacity take max of not taking and taking the item.
Return dp[7].

mistakes.mistake: Iterating capacity forwards in 0/1 knapsack, which allows using an item multiple times.
mistakes.fix: Iterate capacity from high to low in the 0/1 case.

mistakes.mistake: Using capacity as the outer loop in unbounded knapsack and missing item ordering.
mistakes.fix: Loop over items outer, capacity inner, or be deliberate about which variant you implement.

mistakes.mistake: Skipping items heavier than the capacity and forgetting they are valid choices as 'not taken'.
mistakes.fix: dp[c] = dp[c] (unchanged) handles that automatically; just guard the inner loop bound.

problems.name: Target Sum
problems.description: Assign + or - to each integer in nums so the total equals target; count the number of assignments.
hints: Transform into subset-sum with a shifted offset.
Count ways to reach each sum.
problems.approach: Convert to counting subsets: find a subset with sum (total+target)/2.
problems.solution: dp[c] counts ways to reach sum c; process each number with a backwards capacity loop.

problems.name: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.description: Return true if the array can be partitioned into two subsets with equal sums.
problems.approach: Check if any subset sums to half the total using a boolean DP over capacities.
problems.solution: dp[c] is true if a subset sums to c; iterate numbers and capacities backwards.

problems.name: Coin Change 2
problems.description: Count the number of combinations of coins that make up a given amount (unlimited supply).
hints: Order matters for combinations: iterate coins outer.
problems.approach: Unbounded knapsack counting: dp[a] += dp[a-coin] with coins as the outer loop.
problems.solution: Start dp[0]=1; for each coin, for each amount, add dp[amount-coin].

name: Subset Sum
overview: Subset sum asks whether a subset of numbers can add up to a given target. It is a boolean 0/1 knapsack where the value of each item equals its weight, and it underpins partition and target-sum problems.
why: Subset sum is a classic that appears directly or as a reduction in interviews and in many real-world scheduling problems. Recognizing when a problem can be reframed as subset sum is a high-value skill.
when: Reach for subset-sum DP when the question is whether some combination of given numbers can reach an exact total, or when a counting/partition variant asks how many subsets reach a target.

concepts.name: Boolean DP
concepts.description: dp[c] records reachability of sum c, not an optimal value.

concepts.name: Target Bound
concepts.description: Only capacities 0..target are tracked; sums above the target are irrelevant.

concepts.name: Backwards Iteration
concepts.description: Iterating capacity downward keeps each number usable at most once.

concepts.name: Count Variant
concepts.description: dp[c] counts subsets reaching c instead of a boolean flag.

concepts.name: Reduction
concepts.description: Many problems become subset sum after algebra, such as target sum and partition.

patterns.name: Boolean Reachability
patterns.description: Mark each reachable sum by updating from high to low.

patterns.name: Counting Subsets
patterns.description: Count the number of subsets reaching each sum.

examples.title: Subset Sum Reachability
examples.problem: Can a subset of [3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2] sum to 9?
examples.explanation: The boolean table marks 9 reachable because 3+4+2 sums exactly to it.
steps: Initialize dp[0]=True.
Process each number and update capacities downward.
dp[c] becomes true if it was true or dp[c-x] was true.
Return dp[9].

mistakes.mistake: Iterating capacities upward and effectively using numbers multiple times.
mistakes.fix: Use a downward capacity loop for the 0/1 flavor.

mistakes.mistake: Using a huge target and blowing up memory when the sum of all numbers is smaller.
mistakes.fix: Cap the target at the sum of nums since no subset can exceed it.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing counting subsets with counting ordered sequences.
mistakes.fix: Outer loop over numbers (not target) prevents double-counting permutations.

problems.name: Partition Equal Subset Sum
problems.description: Return true if nums can be split into two subsets of equal sum.
problems.approach: Return true only if the total is even and sum/2 is reachable.
problems.solution: Early return false for odd totals, then run boolean subset-sum against total/2.

problems.name: Target Sum
problems.description: Count sign assignments (+/-) that make the numbers sum to a target.
hints: Algebra turns it into a subset sum.
Let P be the positive subset.
problems.approach: Find count of subsets summing to (total + target) / 2.
problems.solution: sum(P) - sum(N) = target implies 2*sum(P) = total + target; count subsets reaching that value.

problems.name: Last Stone Weight II
problems.description: Smash stones so the smallest possible remaining weight is left.
hints: Minimize the difference between two subsets.
Split into the closest two subset sums.
problems.approach: Find the largest subset sum <= total/2; answer is total - 2 * best.
problems.solution: Track reachable sums, take the largest one at most half of total, and compute the remaining gap.

name: Partition DP
overview: Partition DP splits an array or string into contiguous segments, optimizing an objective over the way the cuts are made. The state is an interval (i, j), and the transition tries every possible cut point.
why: Partition DP is a frequent hard-level question pattern covering palindrome partitioning, matrix chain, and burst balloons. It tests whether you can structure a recurrence around sub-intervals and choose a good cut.
when: Reach for partition DP when the problem literally involves cutting, splitting, or partitioning a sequence into parts and optimizing a cost that depends on segment boundaries. The typical state is the start and end of a segment.

concepts.name: Interval State
concepts.description: dp[i][j] represents the optimal answer for the subarray from i to j.

concepts.name: Cut Point
concepts.description: The transition tries every k between i and j as the place to split.

concepts.name: Length Ordering
concepts.description: Processing intervals from small length to large so sub-intervals are ready.

concepts.name: Combining Costs
concepts.description: The answer for an interval combines answers of its left and right parts plus the merge cost.

concepts.name: Palindrome Checking
concepts.description: Precomputing which substrings are palindromes to make transitions cheap.

patterns.name: Min Cuts for Palindrome Partition
patterns.description: Cut into palindromic substrings minimizing the number of cuts.

patterns.name: Burst Balloons / Merge Cost
patterns.description: Choose the order to remove or combine elements to maximize or minimize the total cost.

examples.title: Palindrome Partitioning II
examples.problem: Return the minimum number of cuts needed to split s into palindromic substrings.
examples.explanation: One cut produces two palindromic pieces, which is the minimum.
steps: Precompute is_pal for all substrings.
For each end j, if s[0..j] is a palindrome dp[j]=0.
Otherwise try every split point i and use dp[i]+1 when s[i+1..j] is a palindrome.
Return dp[n-1].

mistakes.mistake: Iterating intervals in the wrong order and using uncomputed sub-intervals.
mistakes.fix: Loop by interval length from small to large.

mistakes.mistake: Recomputing palindrome checks inside the transition, making it O(n^3) unexpectedly.
mistakes.fix: Precompute the palindrome table once.

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one in cut points when counting cuts versus partitions.
mistakes.fix: Clarify whether the answer is the number of cuts or the number of parts and add or subtract one accordingly.

problems.name: Palindrome Partitioning II
problems.description: Return the minimum number of cuts to split s into palindromic substrings.
hints: dp[j] = best cuts for prefix ending at j.
problems.approach: Prefix DP where each transition tries a new palindromic tail.
problems.solution: Use a palindrome table and a prefix cut array; for each j try all palindrome tails ending at j.

problems.name: Burst Balloons
problems.description: Burst balloons for coins equal to the product of neighbors; maximize total coins.
hints: Think of the last balloon burst in an interval.
problems.approach: Pick the last balloon k to burst inside each interval and combine left and right.
problems.solution: Pad with 1s, then for each interval choose k as the final burst, adding nums[i-1]*nums[k]*nums[j+1].

problems.name: Split Array Largest Sum
problems.description: Split the array into k non-empty contiguous subarrays minimizing the largest subarray sum.
hints: dp[i][j] = min max sum for first i elements in j parts.
Binary search on the answer also works.
problems.approach: Try every split point and take the max of prefix sum and remaining parts.
problems.solution: For j parts over i elements, the best is min over splits of max(prefix sum from split, dp[split][j-1]).

name: LCS
overview: Longest Common Subsequence finds the longest subsequence present in two strings while preserving order. It is the canonical example of string DP and a template reused by edit distance, shortest common supersequence, and more.
why: LCS is one of the most asked DP problems and its table structure transfers to many other string comparison problems. Being fluent in its recurrence lets you answer related follow-ups quickly in interviews.
when: Reach for the LCS pattern whenever two sequences must be aligned or compared for shared order-preserving content. Adapt it when you only need the length, the actual subsequence, or a variant cost model.

complexity.space: O(m * n), optimizable to O(min(m, n))

concepts.name: Subsequence vs Substring
concepts.description: Subsequence skips characters and keeps order; substring must be contiguous.

concepts.name: Prefix Table
concepts.description: dp[i][j] is the LCS of the first i and first j characters.

concepts.name: Match Transition
concepts.description: Equal characters extend the LCS by one from the diagonal.

concepts.name: Mismatch Transition
concepts.description: Unequal characters keep the max of dropping one character from either side.

concepts.name: Traceback
concepts.description: Walking the table diagonally and across to recover the actual subsequence.

patterns.name: Classic LCS Length
patterns.description: Fill the prefix table with match/mismatch rules.

patterns.name: LCS as Metric for Other Problems
patterns.description: Derive deletions, supersequence, or similarity from LCS length.
patterns.code:
# min deletions to make a == b from edit ops
# = len(a) + len(b) - 2 * lcs_len(a, b)

examples.title: Longest Common Subsequence
examples.problem: Find the length of the longest subsequence common to 'abcde' and 'ace'.
examples.explanation: Matching a, c, and e in order yields the common subsequence 'ace' of length 3.
steps: Build an (m+1) x (n+1) table initialized to 0.
Loop over each character pair.
On a match, take the diagonal cell plus one.
On a mismatch, take the max of the cell above and the cell to the left.
Return the bottom-right value.

mistakes.mistake: Confusing subsequence with substring and forcing contiguity.
mistakes.fix: Use the skip-either-side recurrence; substring DP is a different problem.

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one indexing between the string and the table rows.
mistakes.fix: Make the table one larger in each dimension and map characters at i-1 and j-1.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to handle empty-prefix rows correctly.
mistakes.fix: Keep row 0 and column 0 as zeros to represent LCS with an empty string.

problems.name: Longest Common Subsequence
problems.description: Return the length of the longest subsequence common to two strings.
problems.approach: Apply the classic LCS recurrence over the full prefix table.
problems.solution: Fill dp[i][j] using the diagonal on match and max of neighbors on mismatch.

problems.name: Delete Operation for Two Strings
problems.description: Return the minimum number of deletions to make two strings equal.
hints: Keep the LCS and delete everything else.
problems.approach: Answer is len(a) + len(b) - 2 * LCS(a, b).
problems.pattern: LCS as Metric for Other Problems
problems.solution: Compute LCS length, then subtract it twice from the sum of the lengths.

problems.name: Shortest Common Supersequence
problems.description: Return the shortest string that has both strings as subsequences.
hints: Reconstruct by walking the LCS table.
problems.approach: Length first, then trace back to build the merged string.
problems.solution: Compute LCS, then build the supersequence by emitting both characters on mismatches and one shared character on matches.

name: LIS
overview: Longest Increasing Subsequence finds the longest subsequence whose elements are strictly increasing. The O(n log n) solution uses a patience-sorting pile array and is a classic interview showcase.
why: LIS appears directly and as a subroutine in problems like Russian doll envelopes and box stacking. Knowing both the O(n^2) and O(n log n) versions demonstrates depth beyond the basic table.
when: Reach for LIS when a problem asks for the longest chain, sequence, or arrangement that must preserve increasing order. If elements must be both increasing in one dimension and sorted in another, use the patience approach on the sorted structure.

complexity.time: O(n^2) naive, O(n log n) optimal

concepts.name: Strict vs Non-Strict
concepts.description: Increasing means strictly greater; non-decreasing allows equal values.

concepts.name: Ends-at State
concepts.description: dp[i] is the LIS length that ends at index i.

concepts.name: Piles Array
concepts.description: tails[k] holds the smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1.

concepts.name: Binary Search Update
concepts.description: Finding the right pile with bisect keeps the process O(n log n).

concepts.name: Follow-up Dimensions
concepts.description: Sorting by one dimension and taking LIS on another handles multi-attribute problems.

patterns.name: O(n^2) LIS
patterns.description: Extend any earlier smaller element's subsequence.

patterns.name: O(n log n) LIS
patterns.description: Binary search the tails array to place each number.

examples.title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
examples.problem: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
examples.explanation: The best increasing subsequence has length 4; the patience array tracks the smallest possible tails.
steps: For the O(n^2) version, init dp[i]=1 and extend from earlier smaller elements.
Return the max of dp.
For the fast version, place each number with bisect_left in the tails array.
Return the length of tails.

mistakes.mistake: Using <= in the comparison and accepting equal elements in a strictly increasing sequence.
mistakes.fix: Use strict < for the increasing condition, or bisect_right for non-decreasing.

mistakes.mistake: Believing the tails array itself is the LIS; it is only a storage structure.
mistakes.fix: Recall that tails is a scaffold; reconstruct the real sequence separately if needed.

mistakes.mistake: Running O(n^2) on a 10^5 input and timing out.
mistakes.fix: Switch to the O(n log n) patience approach for large inputs.

problems.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.description: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: Or use the tails patience array.
problems.approach: Use the O(n log n) patience method for the tight time limit.
problems.solution: Maintain tails with bisect_left and replace or append each element.

problems.name: Russian Doll Envelopes
problems.description: Count the maximum number of envelopes that can be nested inside each other.
hints: LIS on heights with a tie-break.
problems.approach: Sort by width ascending and height descending, then LIS on heights.
problems.solution: Sorting height descending for equal widths prevents false nesting, then apply patience LIS on heights.

problems.name: Number of Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.description: Count the number of longest increasing subsequences.
hints: Track both length and count per index.
Sum counts where length is maximal.
problems.approach: O(n^2) DP keeping length and count for each ending index.
problems.solution: For each i accumulate counts from all earlier j with nums[j] < nums[i], merging equal-length contributions.

name: Edit Distance
overview: Edit distance (Levenshtein distance) is the minimum number of insertions, deletions, and substitutions to convert one string into another. It is the archetype of cost-based string alignment DP.
why: Edit distance is a classic hard question that frequently appears in interviews and is a gateway to autocorrect, diffing, and biological sequence alignment. Its recurrence generalizes to many string-similarity problems.
when: Reach for edit distance when a problem asks for the minimum number of operations to transform one string into another, or for the cost of making two strings equal. Generalize it by changing per-operation costs.

concepts.name: Operations
concepts.description: Insert a character, delete a character, or replace a character, each costing 1.

concepts.name: Prefix State
concepts.description: dp[i][j] is the edit distance between the first i and first j characters.

concepts.name: Base Row and Column
concepts.description: Converting a prefix to empty costs its length in deletions (or insertions).

concepts.name: Match Cost Zero
concepts.description: Equal characters cost nothing and reuse the diagonal value.

concepts.name: Generalization
concepts.description: Weighted costs and other ops like swap extend the same table structure.

patterns.name: Standard Levenshtein
patterns.description: Three-way min over insert, delete, and replace at each cell.

patterns.name: One-Row Optimization
patterns.description: Keep only the previous row and update in place with a saved diagonal.

examples.title: Edit Distance
examples.explanation: Replace h with r, delete the second o, and keep s, for three operations.
steps: Initialize the first row and column with prefix lengths.
Loop over all pairs of characters.
On a match, copy the diagonal; otherwise take 1 plus the min of diagonal, up, and left.
Return the bottom-right cell.

mistakes.mistake: Initializing the table rows and columns to 0 instead of their index lengths.
mistakes.fix: Set dp[i][0]=i and dp[0][j]=j to represent deleting or inserting entire prefixes.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting that a match costs zero and still adding 1.
mistakes.fix: Handle the equality branch separately to copy the diagonal untouched.

mistakes.mistake: Using an O(m*n) table when only the previous row is needed.
mistakes.fix: Switch to the rolling-row implementation.

problems.name: Edit Distance
problems.description: Return the minimum number of insert, delete, and replace operations to convert word1 into word2.
hints: Three operations map to three table neighbors.
problems.approach: Apply the standard Levenshtein recurrence.
problems.solution: Fill the prefix table with a three-way min and a free diagonal on matches.

problems.name: One Edit Distance
problems.description: Return true if the two strings are exactly one edit apart (insert, delete, or replace).
hints: Lengths must differ by at most 1.
Find the first mismatch and check the rest.
problems.approach: A single linear scan plus a tail check avoids building a full table.
problems.solution: Walk both strings; on the first mismatch decide whether an edit fixes the remainder and verify the tail.

problems.name: Delete Operation for Two Strings
problems.description: Return the minimum number of deletions to make two strings identical.
problems.approach: Delete everything not in the LCS: len(a)+len(b)-2*LCS.
problems.solution: Compute the LCS length and subtract twice it from the total length.

name: Matrix Chain Multiplication
overview: Matrix Chain Multiplication finds the parenthesization of a product of matrices that minimizes the total number of scalar multiplications. It is the canonical interval DP where the state is a range of matrices and the transition tries every split point.
why: This problem is a textbook hard-DP question that tests interval recurrences and cost modeling. The template extends directly to problems like optimal binary search trees and burst balloons.
when: Reach for this pattern when a problem asks to combine a sequence of items in some order and the cost depends on which adjacent groups are merged first. The state is the interval of items and the transition is the split point.

concepts.name: Cost of Multiplication
concepts.description: Multiplying p x q by q x r costs p*q*r scalar operations.

concepts.name: Interval State
concepts.description: dp[i][j] is the minimum cost to multiply matrices i through j.

concepts.name: Split Point
concepts.description: The last multiplication splits the chain into a left product and a right product.

concepts.name: Length Ordering
concepts.description: Processing chains by increasing length keeps sub-interval answers ready.

concepts.name: Result Matrix Size
concepts.description: The product of matrices i..j has dimensions dims[i-1] x dims[j].

patterns.name: Classic Interval Min
patterns.description: Minimize over all split points k in (i, j).

examples.title: Optimal Parenthesization
examples.problem: Minimize scalar multiplications for matrices of dimensions [10, 30, 5, 60] (A:10x30, B:30x5, C:5x60).
examples.explanation: (A(BC)) costs 30*5*60 + 10*30*5 = 9000 + 1500 = 10500? No, (BC) costs 30*5*60=9000 giving 30x60, then A*(BC) costs 10*30*60=18000; correct answer is 4500 via (AB)C: A*B costs 10*30*5=1500 giving 10x5, then times C costs 10*5*60=3000, total 4500.
steps: Initialize single-matrix chains to cost 0.
For each chain length, compute every interval's best split.
At each split add left cost, right cost, and the final merge cost.
Return dp[0][n-1].

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one with dimensions since n matrices need n+1 dimension values.
mistakes.fix: Store dims with one extra entry and index matrices 0..n-1.

mistakes.mistake: Processing intervals in an order that reads uncomputed cells.
mistakes.fix: Always iterate by increasing interval length.

mistakes.mistake: Initializing dp[i][i] to infinity and breaking single-matrix base cases.
mistakes.fix: Base case dp[i][i]=0 (no cost to have one matrix).

problems.name: Matrix Chain Multiplication
problems.description: Return the minimum scalar multiplications to multiply a chain of matrices.
problems.approach: For each interval choose the split minimizing combined costs.
problems.solution: Fill dp[i][j] for increasing lengths using dp[i][k]+dp[k+1][j]+dims[i]*dims[k+1]*dims[j+1].

problems.name: Minimum Score Triangulation of Polygon
problems.description: Triangulate a convex polygon minimizing the sum of vertex-value products of all triangles.
hints: Fix a base edge and split into two polygons.
problems.approach: For each interval (i, j) choose a middle vertex k to form a triangle and recurse on both sides.
problems.solution: dp[i][j] = min over k of dp[i][k]+dp[k][j]+values[i]*values[k]*values[j].

problems.name: Burst Balloons
problems.description: Maximize coins collected by bursting balloons in any order, where each burst scores neighbor products.
hints: Reverse the order: think of the last balloon.
problems.approach: Choose the last balloon k in an interval to burst and combine both sides.
problems.solution: Pad with boundary 1s and set dp[i][j] = max over k of coins + dp[i][k-1] + dp[k+1][j].

name: Grid DP
overview: Grid DP computes optimal paths or counts on a matrix where movement follows allowed directions such as down/right. Each cell derives its answer from predecessor cells, making direction of movement the core of the transition.
why: Grid path problems like unique paths, minimum path sum, and dungeon game are common interview questions that test 2D state setup and boundary handling. They also appear with obstacles and variable move sets.
when: Reach for grid DP when you move through a matrix step by step and need to count paths, minimize cost, or check reachability. Determine allowed directions first because they define which neighbors feed each cell.

concepts.name: Movement Directions
concepts.description: Allowed moves (down, right, diagonals, or arbitrary) define the transition neighbors.

concepts.name: Obstacles
concepts.description: Blocked cells contribute zero ways or infinite cost and must be handled in initialization.

concepts.name: Boundary Cells
concepts.description: First row and column have only one predecessor and need special handling.

concepts.name: Grid with Walls
concepts.description: Walls prevent paths; the DP value for wall cells is fixed at 0 or infinity.

concepts.name: Space Reduction
concepts.description: A single row array suffices when each cell only needs the row above and the left neighbor.

patterns.name: Path Counting with Obstacles
patterns.description: Count paths; skip blocked cells.

patterns.name: Max Cost Path
patterns.description: Accumulate the maximum of the possible predecessors.

examples.title: Unique Paths with Obstacles
examples.problem: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right in a grid with obstacles (1) and empty cells (0), moving down or right.
examples.explanation: The obstacle in the middle row forces both valid routes around it, leaving exactly two paths.
steps: Initialize the first cell to 1 if not blocked.
For each cell, if blocked set it to 0.
Otherwise add the path counts from above and left.
Return the bottom-right value.

mistakes.mistake: Not handling the starting cell being an obstacle.
mistakes.fix: Check grid[0][0] before initialization and return 0 if blocked.

mistakes.mistake: Counting paths that pass through obstacles because the blocked cell was seeded with 1.
mistakes.fix: Force blocked cells to 0 before accumulating neighbors.

mistakes.mistake: Using a full matrix when a rolling row is enough, wasting memory on large grids.
mistakes.fix: Keep one row and update it left to right.

problems.name: Unique Paths II
problems.description: Count paths from top-left to bottom-right avoiding obstacles, moving only down or right.
problems.approach: Fill row by row, zeroing blocked cells and adding predecessors otherwise.
problems.solution: Roll a single row array, resetting blocked positions and adding the left neighbor.

problems.name: Minimum Path Sum
problems.description: Return the minimum sum along a path from top-left to bottom-right moving down or right.
hints: Add the smaller of top and left.
First row and column are prefix sums.
problems.approach: Accumulate each cell as its value plus the min of the two predecessors.
problems.space: O(1) when mutating the input grid
problems.solution: Rewrite each cell in place with the min-recurrence so no extra table is needed.

problems.name: Dungeon Game
problems.description: Find the minimum initial health a knight needs to survive a dungeon grid with demons (negative) and health potions (positive).
problems.approach: dp[i][j] is the minimum health needed entering that cell; fill from bottom-right to top-left.
problems.solution: From the exit, required = max(1, 1 - dungeon[i][j] + min(needed below, needed right)) rolling upward.

name: DP on Trees
overview: DP on trees computes answers by combining results from children, using the tree's structure to define natural subproblems. States usually track information about the subtree, often distinguishing whether the current node is chosen or not.
why: Tree DP questions such as house robber III and tree diameters test recursive thinking and memoization over structure. They show up in both medium and hard interviews and are a strong signal of DP maturity.
when: Reach for tree DP when the optimal answer for a node depends on its subtree, or when choosing nodes under adjacency constraints. Solve the subtree bottom-up with a post-order traversal, caching per-node results.

complexity.space: O(n) for the tree and memo

concepts.name: Subtree State
concepts.description: dp[u] describes the optimal answer for the subtree rooted at u.

concepts.name: Choose or Skip
concepts.description: Deciding whether to include u often changes what its children may do.

concepts.name: Post-Order Computation
concepts.description: Computing children first ensures their results exist before combining.

concepts.name: Diameter
concepts.description: The longest path between two nodes, combining the two deepest child chains.

concepts.name: Memoization on Nodes
concepts.description: A dictionary keyed by node reference caches per-node answers in recursion.

patterns.name: House Robber III
patterns.description: Max value choosing non-adjacent nodes in a binary tree.

patterns.name: Tree Diameter
patterns.description: Track the longest path through each node as the two deepest branches.
patterns.code:
def diameter(edges):
    g = {}
    for a, b in edges:
        g.setdefault(a, []).append(b)
        g.setdefault(b, []).append(a)
    best = 0
    def dfs(u, parent):
        nonlocal best
        heights = [dfs(v, u) for v in g[u] if v != parent]
        heights.sort(reverse=True)
        top1 = heights[0] if heights else 0
        top2 = heights[1] if len(heights) > 1 else 0
        best = max(best, top1 + top2)
        return 1 + top1
    dfs(0, -1)
    return best

examples.title: House Robber III
examples.problem: Rob a binary tree of houses so no two directly connected nodes are robbed, maximizing total value.
examples.explanation: The optimal choice skips the root's children but takes the grandchildren, yielding 7.
steps: Define dfs(node) returning (best when node skipped, best when node taken).
For skip, sum the max of each child's two options.
For take, add node.val plus the skip values of both children.
Return max of the root's pair.

mistakes.mistake: Using a single value per node when choosing the node affects children.
mistakes.fix: Return a pair (skip, take) and let the parent combine both.

mistakes.mistake: Processing the parent before the children and using uncomputed values.
mistakes.fix: Guarantee a post-order (children first) traversal.

mistakes.mistake: Following parent pointers and creating cycles in the traversal.
mistakes.fix: Pass the parent down and only visit non-parent neighbors.

problems.name: House Robber III
problems.description: Return the maximum money you can rob from a binary tree without robbing two directly linked houses.
problems.approach: Return (skip, take) from each node's dfs.
problems.solution: skip = max of children pairs summed; take = val + children's skip values; return max at root.

problems.name: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.description: Return the maximum path sum where a path connects any two nodes through their parent links.
hints: A path through a node joins two child branches.
problems.approach: Track the best single branch for each node and the best full path through it.
problems.solution: dfs returns the max downward gain (clamp negatives to 0) while a global tracks node.val + left_gain + right_gain.

problems.name: Binary Tree Cameras
problems.description: Place the minimum cameras so every node is monitored by itself or an adjacent camera.
hints: Greedy bottom-up: cameras go above leaf parents.
problems.approach: Post-order with three states: covered, uncovered, has-camera.
problems.solution: Place cameras at uncovered nodes' parents via post-order recursion, counting each placement.

name: DP on Strings
overview: DP on strings solves problems where subproblems are defined by prefixes or substrings of one or two strings. The state is usually the length of the prefixes involved, and transitions compare characters to decide match, skip, or edit.
why: String DP is among the most common interview categories, covering LCS, edit distance, matching, and segmentation. Being able to frame string problems as prefix comparisons is essential for many medium and hard questions.
when: Reach for string DP when the answer depends on comparing, aligning, or segmenting strings and the state can be expressed with prefix lengths. Precompute tables like palindrome info when substrings are queried repeatedly.

complexity.space: O(m * n), often optimizable to O(n)

concepts.name: Prefix State
concepts.description: dp[i][j] represents the answer for the first i characters of one string and j of the other.

concepts.name: Character Match
concepts.description: Equal characters typically reuse the diagonal state plus a payoff.

concepts.name: Skip Decision
concepts.description: Unequal characters require skipping one side and taking the better result.

concepts.name: Substring Queries
concepts.description: Problems on substrings often precompute is-palindrome or cost tables.

concepts.name: Reconstruction
concepts.description: Tracing back through the table to recover an actual string rather than just a number.

patterns.name: Wildcard / Regex Matching
patterns.description: Match patterns where * matches any sequence and ? matches one character.

patterns.name: Palindromic Substring Table
patterns.description: Precompute which substrings are palindromes for O(1) queries.

examples.title: Longest Palindromic Substring
examples.problem: Find the longest contiguous substring that reads the same forwards and backwards.
examples.explanation: The palindrome table marks palindromic substrings; the longest has length 3.
steps: Build the palindrome table with single characters as true.
For each substring, check the ends and the interior.
Track the longest true substring.
Return that substring.

mistakes.mistake: Treating substring and subsequence the same in the recurrence.
mistakes.fix: Substrings are contiguous: transitions only extend adjacent characters.

mistakes.mistake: Off-by-one between character indexes and table rows.
mistakes.fix: Use an (m+1) x (n+1) table and map characters at i-1, j-1.

mistakes.mistake: Filling palindrome tables top-down instead of bottom-up by substring length.
mistakes.fix: Iterate i from the end so interior palindromes are computed first.

problems.name: Longest Palindromic Substring
problems.description: Return the longest palindromic contiguous substring of s.
problems.approach: Either center expansion in O(n^2) or a DP palindrome table.
problems.space: O(n^2), or O(1) with center expansion
problems.solution: Mark single chars as palindromes, then extend by matching ends while tracking the longest.

problems.name: Interleaving String
problems.description: Return true if s3 is formed by interleaving s1 and s2 preserving each one's order.
hints: State is (i, j) pointers into s1 and s2.
problems.approach: dp[i][j] is true if s3[:i+j] is an interleaving of s1[:i] and s2[:j].
problems.solution: Seed dp[0][0], then extend by consuming a character from s1 or s2 when it matches s3.

problems.name: Distinct Subsequences
problems.description: Count the number of distinct ways s can form t as a subsequence.
hints: On match you may skip or use the character.
problems.solution: On a match add the skip case and the take case; otherwise carry the skip case.

name: Bitmask DP
overview: Bitmask DP uses an integer whose bits represent which elements are already used, turning subsets into states. It solves assignment, scheduling, and TSP-style problems that need to remember a set of choices, typically in O(2^n * n).
why: Bitmask DP appears in hard interview problems and coding contests when the state must encode an entire subset. Knowing it signals fluency in advanced DP and is especially valued for onsite rounds.
when: Reach for bitmask DP when n is small (typically <= 20) and the decision depends on which items were already chosen, such as partitioning, assignment, or shortest Hamiltonian path. Encode the used-set as the bitmask.

concepts.name: Mask as State
concepts.description: An integer where bit k is set if element k has been used.

concepts.name: Bit Operations
concepts.description: Setting, clearing, and checking bits with OR, AND, and shifts.

concepts.name: Subset Iteration
concepts.description: Enumerating all submasks or all masks up to 2^n.

concepts.name: n Limit
concepts.description: Feasible only for n up to about 20 due to the 2^n state space.

concepts.name: Transition on One Bit
concepts.description: Adding an unused element by OR-ing in its bit.

patterns.name: Minimum Assignment Cost
patterns.description: Assign n items to n slots minimizing total cost.

patterns.name: Hamiltonian Path
patterns.description: Shortest path visiting every node exactly once, ending anywhere.

examples.title: Minimum Number of Work Sessions
examples.problem: Assign n tasks to the fewest sessions of capacity sessionTime.
examples.explanation: One session fits [3] and another fits [1, 2], so two sessions suffice.
steps: Represent each subset of tasks as a bitmask.
Store (sessions, used_time) for each mask.
Try adding each task not yet in the mask.
Return the session count for the full mask.

mistakes.mistake: Running bitmask DP when n is 30+, exceeding the 2^n limit.
mistakes.fix: Confirm n <= 20; otherwise look for a greedy or polynomial approach.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting to initialize dp[0] and mis-indexing the mask size.
mistakes.fix: Allocate arrays of size 1 << n and always seed the empty mask.

mistakes.mistake: Iterating masks without a meaningful order, breaking transitions.
mistakes.fix: Process masks by increasing bit count or rely on the fact that OR-ing a bit increases the mask value.

problems.name: Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets
problems.description: Return true if the array can be partitioned into k subsets of equal sum.
hints: Each subset must reach target = sum / k.
problems.approach: DFS over masks tracking which numbers are used and the current subset total.
problems.solution: Memoize by mask; fill subsets one at a time and count completed subsets.

problems.name: Shortest Path Visiting All Nodes
problems.description: Return the shortest path length visiting every node of a graph, revisiting allowed.
problems.approach: BFS where each state is (visited-mask, node), with Floyd-Warshall for distances.
problems.solution: Run BFS from every start node expanding to unvisited neighbors until the full mask is reached.

problems.name: Maximum Number of Groups Getting Fresh Donuts
problems.description: Order batches so the maximum number of groups are satisfied after a fixed-size batch cycle.
hints: Group sizes matter only modulo batchSize.
Counts per remainder fit in a mask-based memo.
problems.approach: Bitmask DP over remainder counts with memoization.
problems.solution: Memoize on the tuple of remaining counts and current total remainder to maximize satisfied groups.

name: Digit DP
overview: Digit DP counts or sums numbers in a range by processing digits one at a time, with a tight flag tracking whether the prefix already equals the upper bound. It answers questions like how many numbers in [L, R] satisfy a digit property.
why: Digit DP is a specialized but frequently asked hard pattern for range-counting questions involving digit properties. Mastering its tight/safe state construction lets you solve counting problems that naive iteration cannot.
when: Reach for digit DP when the problem asks to count or sum integers within a range satisfying conditions on their digits, such as containing no repeated digits or having digits sum to a target. Convert [L, R] to f(R) - f(L-1).

concepts.name: Tight Flag
concepts.description: A boolean saying the prefix matches the limit so far, restricting upcoming digits.

concepts.name: Leading Zero Handling
concepts.description: Deciding whether to allow leading zeros that would not count as digits.

concepts.name: Range Decomposition
concepts.description: answer(L, R) = count(R) - count(L-1).

concepts.name: Digit Property State
concepts.description: Extra parameters encoding the property, like last digit or running sum.

concepts.name: Memoization over Positions
concepts.description: Caching on (position, tight, property-state) makes the search polynomial.

patterns.name: Count with No Consecutive Digits
patterns.description: Classic digit DP with tight flag and previous-digit state.

patterns.name: Range Difference Trick
patterns.description: Convert inclusive range queries into two prefix counts.
patterns.code:
def count_range(lo, hi, pred):
    return pred(hi) - pred(lo - 1)

examples.title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
examples.problem: Count integers from 0 to n that have no repeated digits.
examples.explanation: Iterating would be too slow, but digit DP counts valid numbers by position with a used-digits mask.
steps: Convert the bound into its digit string.
Recurse position by position with a tight flag.
Track which digits have been used in a bitmask.
Memoize on (pos, tight, used) and sum valid counts.

mistakes.mistake: Forgetting the tight flag and counting numbers larger than the bound.
mistakes.fix: Carry tight and only allow digits up to the bound digit when tight is set.

mistakes.mistake: Not converting [L, R] into prefix counts and double-counting.
mistakes.fix: Always compute count(R) - count(L-1).

mistakes.mistake: Treating leading zeros as significant digits and wrongly rejecting valid short numbers.
mistakes.fix: Add a started flag or handle the zero prefix specially.

problems.name: Numbers At Most N Given Digit Set
problems.description: Count positive integers up to n whose digits come only from a given set.
hints: Equal-length numbers use a tight pass.
problems.approach: Count all lengths below the bound, then digit-DP the equal-length case.
problems.solution: For shorter lengths use k^len; for the full length simulate digit choices with a tight flag.

problems.name: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
problems.description: Count integers in [0, n] with no repeated digits.
problems.approach: Digit DP tracking used digits with a tight flag.
problems.solution: Recurse over positions, forbidding reuse of digits via a mask and respecting tightness.

problems.name: Count of Integers
problems.description: Count integers between num1 and num2 whose digit sum is between min_sum and max_sum.
hints: Digit sum state plus tight flag.
problems.approach: Digit DP on both bounds with a digit-sum state.
problems.solution: Compute count(<=X) minus count(<num1) via memoized digit DP constrained by digit sum bounds.

name: Dynamic Programming
overview: Dynamic programming solves problems by breaking them into overlapping subproblems, computing each once, and combining the results. It applies wherever an optimal solution can be built from optimal solutions of smaller subproblems.
why: DP is one of the most heavily tested categories across all interview levels. Demonstrating a clear recurrence, correct base cases, and proper complexity analysis is a reliable differentiator for candidates.
when: Reach for DP when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure: the answer repeats smaller versions of itself, and combining optimal sub-answers yields the optimal overall answer. Start with brute force, then identify the state and recurrence.

complexity.time: Varies by state count: O(n), O(n^2), or O(n^3)
complexity.space: Varies; often optimizable to O(1) or O(n)

concepts.name: Optimal Substructure
concepts.description: An optimal solution contains optimal solutions to its subproblems.

concepts.name: Overlapping Subproblems
concepts.description: The same subproblem recurs many times, motivating caching.

concepts.name: State Definition
concepts.description: The minimal parameters that uniquely identify a subproblem.

concepts.name: Recurrence Relation
concepts.description: The equation expressing a state in terms of smaller states.

concepts.name: Top-Down vs Bottom-Up
concepts.description: Memoized recursion versus iterative table filling, chosen per problem.

concepts.name: Space Optimization
concepts.description: Reducing memory by keeping only the states actually needed.

patterns.name: State + Recurrence Template
patterns.description: Identify the state, write the recurrence, seed base cases, then memoize or tabulate.
patterns.code:
def solve(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    dp = [0] * (n + 1)
    dp[0] = 0
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        # replace with the problem's recurrence
        dp[i] = max(dp[i - 1], nums[i - 1])
    return dp[n]

patterns.name: Brute Force to DP
patterns.description: Write the naive recursion, detect repeated states, then add a cache.

examples.title: Climbing Stairs
examples.problem: Count distinct ways to climb n stairs taking 1 or 2 steps.
examples.explanation: Ways follow the Fibonacci pattern: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5 for steps 0..4.
steps: Define state dp[i] as ways to reach step i.
Write the recurrence dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2].
Seed base cases dp[0] = 1 and dp[1] = 1.
Fill iteratively and return dp[n].

mistakes.mistake: Jumping straight to code without defining the state and recurrence.
mistakes.fix: Write the state and recurrence in words or pseudocode first.

mistakes.mistake: Missing base cases and letting the table drift.
mistakes.fix: Verify the first two or three values by hand against the recurrence.

mistakes.mistake: Choosing the wrong state so subproblems are not actually overlapping.
mistakes.fix: Confirm that smaller states recur and that combining them preserves optimality.

problems.name: House Robber
problems.description: Return the maximum money robbed without taking two adjacent houses.
problems.approach: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]) with rolling variables.
problems.solution: Track two rolling values: skip the current house or take it plus the value two houses back.

problems.name: Coin Change
problems.description: Return the fewest coins needed to make an amount, or -1 if impossible.
hints: Try every coin as the last one.
problems.approach: dp[a] = 1 + min over coins of dp[a - coin], iterating amounts up.
problems.solution: Fill dp from 0 to amount, taking the minimum over valid coin subtractions.

problems.name: Longest Increasing Subsequence
problems.description: Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: dp[i] is the length ending at i.
problems.approach: Use O(n log n) patience sort or O(n^2) DP.
problems.solution: Maintain the tails array with binary search, appending or replacing per element.
